title: Industrial Property Identification
name: Industrial Property Identification
metaTitle: Industrial Property Identification in San Diego, CA
metaDescription: Industrial replacement property identification for San Diego exchanges, checking FTZ, CBP, and environmental status that a listing sheet often skips.

sections.html: Industrial replacement property in San Diego runs from Kearny Mesa flex space to border-adjacent warehouse and distribution buildings near Otay Mesa, and the listing sheet for any of it tends to lead with clear-height, dock doors, and asking rent. What it often does not lead with is whether the building sits inside a foreign-trade zone, what its environmental history looks like, or whether its lease roll includes defense-contractor tenants with their own assignment requirements.

sections.heading: What the Listing Sheet Leaves for You to Find Out Later
sections.html: A property marketed as border-industrial near Otay Mesa may or may not carry active foreign-trade zone status, and that status affects how a tenant's customs and duty obligations work, which in turn affects lease value and tenant retention. Environmental history on older industrial stock, particularly buildings with a manufacturing or fuel-storage past, is another item that shows up in a Phase I report, not in the marketing flyer. Identifying a property without checking either one is identifying a building you do not fully understand yet.

sections.heading: Screening Candidates Before They Go on the Letter
sections.html: Before an industrial property goes on a 45-day identification letter, we check title, environmental flags, zoning consistency with the current or intended use, and lease terms on any in-place tenant. Defense and Navy-adjacent tenants in San Diego industrial buildings sometimes carry longer lead times for landlord consent on assignment, which matters if the closing timeline is tight.

sections.heading: Why Otay Mesa and the Port Corridor Trade Differently
sections.html: Demand along San Diego's border-industrial corridor is driven by cross-border logistics and manufacturing tied to trade flow through Otay Mesa, which behaves differently than a typical infill industrial submarket. Vacancy can be thin even when rents look soft on paper, because tenants value the specific customs and trade-zone advantages of a location more than square footage alone. A comparable pulled from a different submarket can understate what a border-adjacent building is actually worth.

sections.heading: The Screening Checklist for Every Candidate
sections.html:
Every industrial candidate we bring forward for a San Diego exchange gets checked against the same list:

  • Foreign-trade zone or customs bonded warehouse status, if applicable
  • Environmental Phase I history and any flagged conditions
  • Zoning consistency with current and intended use
  • In-place lease terms and tenant assignment requirements
  • Clear-height, dock configuration, and power capacity against the intended use

sections.heading: Where Your Own Diligence Still Matters
sections.html: Screening narrows the field to candidates worth pursuing seriously. It does not replace your own inspection, a Phase II environmental study if flags are raised, or legal review of any existing lease or customs arrangement. Confirm final findings with the appropriate specialist before closing.

sections.heading: How a Listing Broker's Comp Set Can Overstate Demand
sections.html:
An industrial listing pitched with a strong comp set sometimes leans on sales from a different corridor entirely, a Miramar or Sorrento Valley trade compared against a candidate near Otay Mesa, because the raw square-footage numbers line up even though the tenant base and demand drivers do not. Cross-border logistics tenants price space differently than tenants serving a purely local distribution radius, and treating the two as interchangeable inflates what a candidate is actually worth.

We pull comps from the same functional corridor as the candidate itself before an identification decision gets made, rather than accepting a broker's assembled set at face value.

The same discipline applies to vacancy figures. A submarket-wide vacancy rate can look tight even when the specific building type an investor needs, refrigerated, high-power, or bonded warehouse space, is actually oversupplied or undersupplied relative to the headline number.

Ask any broker presenting a comp set which candidates share the property's specific power capacity, clear height, and access requirements, rather than accepting a broader industrial classification as a stand-in for those details.

A property that looks comparable on a data sheet can be functionally unusable for a specific tenant's operation if the power capacity or clear height falls short, which is a detail no generic comp report is built to catch on its own.

These specifics matter most for tenants with real operational requirements, cold storage, heavy manufacturing, bonded warehouse use, where a mismatch on any one item can rule out a candidate entirely regardless of how well it compares on price.

Confirming these specifics before a property goes on the identification letter is far cheaper than discovering the mismatch after closing, when the only options left are an expensive retrofit or a tenant who cannot actually occupy the space as planned.

faqs.q: Why does foreign-trade zone status matter for a San Diego industrial replacement property?
faqs.a: It affects tenant customs and duty obligations, which can influence lease value and tenant retention along the Otay Mesa border corridor. It rarely appears on a standard listing sheet.

faqs.q: Do older San Diego industrial buildings carry environmental risk?
faqs.a: Some do, particularly buildings with a manufacturing or fuel-storage history. A Phase I environmental report, not the marketing flyer, is where that history actually shows up.

faqs.q: Why does defense-adjacent tenancy add a step to industrial identification?
faqs.a: Some defense-contractor and Navy-adjacent leases carry specific assignment and consent requirements beyond a standard commercial lease, which can affect closing timing if not identified early.

faqs.q: Are Otay Mesa industrial comps reliable if pulled from a different San Diego submarket?
faqs.a: Not always. Border-adjacent industrial trades on customs and trade-zone advantages as much as square footage, so a comparable from an unrelated submarket can misstate actual value.

faqs.q: Does property screening replace a Phase II environmental study?
faqs.a: No. Screening flags concerns worth investigating further. A formal Phase II or legal review still needs to happen through the appropriate specialist before closing.
